ucldc_schema:description.item: UCI student protest that occurred in April 1993 over the absence of an Asian American Studies Program. Over 200 students rallied outside the administration building (Aldrich Hall) and then marched inside. The video contains news coverage, footage of the rally, protest and march, and student interviews. These efforts led to the creation of a Department of Asian American Studies.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Leslie Ann Bishop is a senior medical officer in obstetrics and gynaecology with the Scarborough Hospital in Tobago. She completed her undergraduate medical training at the University of the West Indies. She also completed a Diploma in anathesia and five years of postgraduate training in Obstetric and Gynaeology in the United Kingdom. She discusses the benefits and risks of homebirths.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Access to this film is generously supported by funding from the National Film Preservation Foundation.

Shows ground-breaking and opening ceremonies of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company's West Adams Los Angeles home office. Co-founder Norman Houston and colleague looking at blueprints. Installation of murals painted by Charles Alston and Hale Woodruff. Grand opening includes ribbon cutting ceremony and unveiling of the mural and the bust of founder William Nickerson, Jr. Also shown, the placement of the time capsule and cornerstone. Documentation on film leader indicates "Original to be used for reprint only."

ucldc_schema:description.item: This story was told by an assistant professor of Gender and Sexuality Studies at UCI. The narrator describes her childhood educational experiences and the inaccurate, harmful portrayals of African American history, culture, and life by the education system and mainstream media. She also discusses her work on Black feminism and sexuality, how she developed an interest in the work, and how she implements these concepts into her own teachings. Warning: story touches on the topic of sexual violence, though not graphically or in depth.
This story includes a video file of the interview and transcript.
Metadata creation for this item was supported through a Confronting Extremism Program awarded through the Office of Inclusive Excellence.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Access to this material is generously supported by funding from the John Randolph Haynes and Dora Haynes Foundation.

Produced by Emma E. Pullen and narrated by the actress, Nichelle Nichols, Marcing into the Millenium presents a brief history of African Americans in Los Angeles. Councilman Mark Ridley-Thomas, and Councilwoman Rita Waters, Councilwoman Ruth Galanter, Mayor Tom Bradley, Rick Moss of the California African American Museum, LA County Supervisor Yvonne Burke, and Mayor Richard Riordan, among others, are featured in this presentation. The founding of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company begins around the 4 minute mark. This film also includes discussions about Biddy Mason and Miriam Matthews.

ucldc_schema:description.item: A circa 1953 filmed tour of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company West Adams home office shortly after it was built. Footage shows staffers at work in various departments, a detailed view of the office interiors and equipment and installation of a sign publicizing a new hospital plan. A number of key personnel appear such as Helen Batiste, Edgar J. Johnston, Ivan Houston, Verna Hickman, and co-founders George Beavers and Norman Houston. Also shown are Bertha Nickerson, Lena Horne, and Joe Louis.
Access to this film is generously supported by funding from the National Film Preservation Foundation.

ucldc_schema:description.item: One of only two surviving examples in the collection of an annual outdoor event held for staffers and their families, celebrating the 1925 founding of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company. The films are significant because they show local recreation sites frequented by African Americans during segregation. Over the years Golden State Mutual picnics were held at Val Verde (known as the “Black Palm Springs”), Santa Monica Beach between Bay and Bicknel streets (colloquially referred to as “The Ink Spot” or “Ink Well Beach”), Cabrillo Beach and Lake Elsinore. This footage was shot near Val Verde.
Access to this film is generously supported by funding from the National Film Preservation Foundation.

ucldc_schema:description.item: This story was told by an Ethnic Studies educator from Los Angeles. This story discusses the narrator's educational experiences growing up and as an educator, and how her Chicana identity has influenced her experiences over time. In regards to her work, the narrator talks about California's Assembly Bill 101, which mandates ethnic studies as a graduation requirement for high schoolers, and her role in developing the curriculum and co-founding the Liberated Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum Coalition. This video is part 1 of 2.
This story includes two video files for the same interview, two transcripts to accompany each video file, and an abstract for the story.
Metadata creation for this item was supported through a Confronting Extremism Program awarded through the Office of Inclusive Excellence.

ucldc_schema:description.item: An oral history with Hailee Van Housen from Bakersfield, California. She has been a teacher for 2 years; her first year, she taught 1st grade and the 2019-2020 academic school year is her first time teaching kindergarten. During the interview, she discusses her experience teaching kindergarten remotely as the local public schools remain closed due to the Coronavirus Pandemic. She talks about many topics relating to remote learning regarding kindergarteners, including her students academic process, her teaching style, how she has maintained connections with both her students and their parents, etc.

ucldc_schema:description.item: An oral history with Lisa Speakman from Bakersfield, California. She is a kindergarten teacher from Stine Elementary School and has taught there for 2 years. She has been teaching kindergarten for about 30 years overall. During this interview, Mrs. Speakman discussed her overall experience having to teach kindergarten remotely as the schools in the city temporarily closed due to the Coronavirus Pandemic. She recalls what she has seen on her screen during her Zoom sessions with the kindergarten students, how teaching remotely has affected her teaching style, how her students have fared with learning through zoom, and other related topics.

ucldc_schema:description.item: This story was told by a person who is currently pursuing her doctorate in psychology. The narrator discusses the difficulties of navigating higher education as a first-generation Latinx college student at UCI. She comments on the socioeconomic disparities that she has noticed during university and what she aspires to do for her community through her career.
This story includes an audio file, transcript, and time log.
Metadata creation for this item was supported through a Confronting Extremism Program awarded through the Office of Inclusive Excellence.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Access to this film is generously supported by funding from the National Film Preservation Foundation.

One of only two surviving examples in the collection of an annual outdoor event held for staffers and their families, celebrating the 1925 founding of the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company. The films are significant because they show local recreation sites frequented by African Americans during segregation. Over the years Golden State Mutual picnics were held at Val Verde (known as the “Black Palm Springs”), Santa Monica Beach between Bay and Bicknel streets (colloquially referred to as “The Ink Spot” or “Ink Well Beach”), Cabrillo Beach and Lake Elsinore.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Jade Drakes never considered having a child before meeting her current partner. She is now the mother of two boys. She experienced severe nausea up until the 8 month of her pregnancy. Because her blood type is A negative, she sought medical care very early in her pregnancy.  She accessed health care at the Port of Spain General Hospital as she resides in Belmont which is a short distance away. She and her partner took birthing classes at the public hospital and Mamatoto Resource and Birth Centre. She shares her experiences pre and post post-delivery.

ucldc_schema:description.item: The audio-visual project "The City is a Body" developed and created by Farah Hamade, the 2020 UCSF Library Artist in Residence,  discusses COVID-19 disparities in San Francisco. ucldc_schema:description.item: Masika Lewis is a mother in 20s, who resides in Carenage, Trinidad. She has a son who is 19 months. She and her partner and their son live with her parents. During the interview she discusses how she felt when she first learned she was pregnant. She talks about her familiarity with what to expect as her mom is a midwife with the Mamatoto Resource and Birth Centre. She shares how she selected her OBGYN. She felt she had a good pregnancy with no overt symptoms such as nausea or swollen feet.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Lisa Hernandez is employed with the North Central regional Health Authority, who lives Brasso Seco, Trinidad. She is the mother of five children, three boys and two girls, the oldest being 23 and the youngest 3. She is also the grandmother of 4 children, whose ages range from 4-6.  She observed two home births. One of these births was a stillbirth. All of her children were delivered at the Mt. Hope Women’s Hospital, Champs Fleurs, Trinidad. Her first birth was the most difficult, but her last child was delivered via C-section. She recounts her experiences before and after giving birth.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Contains one documentary film entitled, "The 2%: Navigating UCI as a Black Student" (2020). The documentary was directed and produced by Iyanna Blackburn (class of 2022), a third-year double major in Film & Media Studies and African American Studies at the University of California, Irvine. The documentary focuses on the perspectives of Black students at UCI. Students share personal experiences of what it is like to navigate the UCI campus, given that the Black student demographic on campus is less than two percent. The documentary was produced while Blackburn was an intern at Anteater TV.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Ayonna Ferreira-Lee is a 25-year-old mother from Sangre Grande, Trinidad. She admits to being quite emotional when she first learned that she was pregnant.  Soon after learning about her pregnancy, she joined the pre-natal clinic at the Sangre Grande Hospital, which is located in Sangre Grande, the largest town in northeast Trinidad. She was put on sick leave due to the severe morning sickness she experienced up to 20 weeks into her pregnancy. The doctors ordered frequent ultrasounds to monitor the health of her baby. Despite the morning sickness, she enjoyed the preparation leading up to the birth of her daughter. She describes her pregnancy as bittersweet.

ucldc_schema:description.item: After a majority of workers at the New Otani Hotel in downtown Los Angeles supported unionization, hotel management refused to negotiate. Members of HERE Local 11 from other Los Angeles hotels pledged to support the New Otani workers with weekly demonstrations that escalated into long-lasting boycott. This 1996 video produced by HERE Local 11 documents the union's strategy of targeting the Kajima Corporation, a large Japanese construction firm that was the major stakeholders in the New Otani, which led to alliances with Japanese trade unionists and the Japanese-American community in Los Angeles. An example of "corporate campaigns" that many unions mounted in the 1980s, the boycott campaign focused on Kajima's role in mid-century Japanese military expansion, the privatization of public services in Japan during the 1980s, and the public development subsidies Los Angeles had provided to Kajima and its partners. The film ends with scenes of a large act of nonviolent civil disobedience in the streets outside the hotel.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Access to this material is generously supported by funding from the John Randolph Haynes and Dora Haynes Foundation.

The video provides an an overview of the Golden State Minority Foundation, which was established in 1974. Interviews include: Ivan A. Houston, executive director, Golden State Minority Foundation; Rosa Flores, vice president, La Salle Partners, and a former scholarship recipient; R. Neil Cheatham, chairman, Robert Vance Securities, and former scholarship recipient; Steven Bell, Angeles, Mesa Elementary School; Alexandra Hart, Peacock Players. Also discussed is the Educational Enrichment Support Project, an initiative to assist local K-12 students that was initiated following the 1992 Los Angeles unrest.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Oral history of Mr. Huynh Van Chinh, who also goes by the name of Trung Chinh. He was born in My Tho, Vietnam in 1943 and was a medical doctor of the Army 1971 until the war ended in 1975. During the interview he described his experience growing up in a poor family, his schooling, and then his time in the Army. When the war ended, he was sent to reeducation camp for one year, released to work at a hospital in ChoLon and then escaped Vietnam by boat and passed through  Pulau Bidong, Malaysia. He resettled in Denver, Colorado through a sponsor. In 2000, he came to settle down in Los Angeles, California.

In 2008, the Vietnamese American community in Austin, along with VAHF, successfully collaborated with the University of Texas at Austin’s Center For Asian American Studies (CAAS) to establish a course on Vietnamese American history and culture, instructed by Ph.D. candidate Linda Ho Peché. Each student was required to complete an oral interview of a self-identified Vietnamese American. These oral histories became part of the 500 Oral History Project initiated by VAHF as its third most urgent collection, since many members of the first genera- tion of Vietnamese Americans are now elderly. With their passing, first-hand accounts of the Vietnamese American immigration experience would be lost.

ucldc_schema:description.item: An oral history with Mr. Phu Do Nguyen, a lawyer and father of three. He was born in 1965 in Saigon and he escaped Vietnam by boat as an unaccompanied minor. This interview focused on his experience as a Vietnamese refugee and how that molded his character, to his thought processes and way of life as a patriotic American. He joined the American military and earned his law degree in the U.S. His message to future generations is, “Do what you love, not for the money. If you do something you love and you’re passionate about it, the money will come because you are so good at it. Do what you love.”

In 2008, the Vietnamese American community in Austin, along with VAHF, successfully collaborated with the University of Texas at Austin’s Center For Asian American Studies (CAAS) to establish a course on Vietnamese American history and culture, instructed by Ph.D. candidate Linda Ho Peché. Each student was required to complete an oral interview of a self-identified Vietnamese American. These oral histories became part of the 500 Oral History Project initiated by VAHF as its third most urgent collection, since many members of the first genera- tion of Vietnamese Americans are now elderly. With their passing, first-hand accounts of the Vietnamese American immigration experience would be lost.

ucldc_schema:description.item: This educational video documents UCSF Moffitt Hospital’s innovative “Care Through Parents” program, which allowed parents to stay overnight with hospitalized children under age 5. The program addresses the critical need for emotional continuity during pediatric hospitalization, recognizing that separation from parents can be more traumatic for young children than their medical condition. Narrated by Carol Hardgrove, M.A., Assistant Clinical Professor of Family Health Care Nursing at UCSF, this program serves as both a case study of successful healthcare innovation and a practical guide for other hospitals seeking to implement similar family-centered pediatric care models.

The preservation and digitization of this resource were supported by a Recordings at Risk grant from the Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR). The grant program is made possible by funding from the Mellon Foundation.

ucldc_schema:description.item: The Los Angeles Living Wage Coalition explains the fight to extend the city's living wage ordinance to workers at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). This 1998 production features interviews with Madeline Janis-Aparicio (LAANE) and Jackie Goldberg (L.A. City Counsel) as well as scenes of Mike Garcia leading a protest by SEIU Local 1877 at LAX. Rank-and-file workers explain the struggle of living in L.A. while earning low wages.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Andrew Dumm is 36 years old and works as a Project Manager/Accounts Payable/Purchasing Manager for Custom Copper Sheet Metal Roofing. He works and lives in his hometown Roseville, CA. He has lived in the greater Sacramento suburban area his whole life. He has a wife, Stephanie Dumm, and two children. In this interview, he describes his personal beliefs on COVID-19: the government is not doing enough and the issue is over-politicized. Andrew goes on to describe his workplace environment and how it has been altered by COVID-19, as well as the roofing industry as a whole. He talks about how his family has managed during the pandemic, and how he and his wife have struggled to find the places and resources to go on dates. He goes on to discuss how he eventually reached an emotional breaking point during the pandemic and ended up seeking out help from mental health professionals. Finally, he discusses his new and beloved hobby in 3D modeling/printing he has acquired due to being home more under the pandemic.

ucldc_schema:description.item: This is a story about resilience, reflected in the lived experiences and voices of two Latina women who had been made to feel like outsiders during their youth. This story discusses their experiences with prejudice and discrimination, their identity as Latina women who also became teen moms, and their opinions on ethnic studies in education.

This story includes a poem written by the creator and based on her personal life, as well as a video file, transcript, and time log for an interview with Marbella Camargo, an undergraduate studying psychology at California State University, Fullerton.
Metadata creation for this item was supported through a Confronting Extremism Program awarded through the Office of Inclusive Excellence.

ucldc_schema:description.item: Nadia is a mother of three from Scarborough, Tobago. Her eldest child is 17 and the youngest is 2 weeks old. With her last child she experienced extreme morning sickeness. She recounts in detail the birth experience of her last child. She couldnt remember the birth of her first although she remembered that the baby weght 10 pounds and for her second child she recalled that the doctor had to induce labour because the baby was overdue.
